item.title: The Hidden Cost of Transparency: How Evaluator Stance Shapes Feedback Responses among Individual Platform Participants
item.description:
Meeting room 4.4, Level 4. School of Computing and Information Systems 1, Singapore Management University, 80 Stamford Road, Singapore 178902 Monday, November 23, 2026, 2 - 2:30pm
The Hidden Cost of Transparency: How Evaluator Stance Shapes Feedback Responses among Individual Platform Participants
Platforms increasingly reveal who evaluated a contribution and with what stance, but little is known about how this transparency shapes recipients, who often decide for themselves whether to act on feedback. We distinguish feedback content from the evaluative signal and examine how an evaluator's revealed stance shapes recipients' responses to feedback using two field studies. The first, on an online healthcare platform, finds that evaluative stance matters: physicians improve service performance after receiving positive patient reviews, whereas negative reviews produce no significant improvement. The second isolates the effect of evaluator stance on a crowdsourcing platform where voting shifted from anonymous to attributable while substantive feedback remained unchanged. Once evaluators’ stances become visible, ideators become less likely to incorporate suggestions from detractors, while incorporation of suggestions from supporters, non-voters, and ideators themselves remains unaffected. These findings show that negative evaluative signals can weaken receptiveness to substantive feedback, highlighting an important hidden cost of platform transparency.
This is a Pre-Conference talk for 2026 Pre-ICIS SIGDSA Symposium (SIGDSA 2026): https://preicis.sigdsa.org/.
More info: computing.smu.edu.sg…: https://computing.smu.edu.sg/newsletter/pre-conference-talk-liaw-shao-yi-hidden-cost-transparency-how-evaluator-stance-shapes?newsletter

item.title: Should we balance? A preliminary study into the maintainability of formal specifications as Linux kernel source code evolves
item.description:
Meeting Room 4-4, Level 4. SMU SCIS 1, Singapore 178902 Monday, November 23, 2026, 5 - 6pm
Should we balance? A preliminary study into the maintainability of formal specifications as Linux kernel source code evolves
Today there is a renewed interest in formal verification of software, in part to thoroughly check that AI-generated code does what it was intended to do, and in part in recognition that critical code bases are becoming increasingly complex and a better understanding of their behavior is needed. Still, verifying a single code instance is not sufficient. It is also necessary to ensure that the code remains verifiable as it evolves. In this talk, we consider the latter problem in the context of a function used in the Linux kernel task scheduler. We find that simple changes in the code require only minor adjustments to the specifications and the verification process. More complex changes, however, can trigger situations that challenge the underlying SMT solvers used to make verification tractable. But we find that code inducing such challenging situations may also harbor bugs. The talk is based on the joint work with Keisuke Nishimura and Jean-Pierre Lozi presented at SAS 2024.
More info: computing.smu.edu.sg…: https://computing.smu.edu.sg/newsletter/research-seminar-julia-lawall-should-we-balance-preliminary-study-maintainability-formal?newsletter

Julia LAWALL Senior Research Scientist Inria Paris
Julia LAWALL received the Ph.D. degree in 1994 from the Indiana University. She has been a senior research scientist at Inria since 2011 and head of the Whisper team since 2021. Previously, she was an Associate Professor at the University of Copenhagen. Her research interests are in the area of improving the quality of infrastructure software, using a variety of approaches including program analysis, program transformation, and software verification. She develops the tool Coccinelle that is extensively used in the development of the Linux kernel and she has over 2000 patches in the Linux kernel based on this work.

item.title: Innovative Wearable Acoustic Sensing Mechanisms for Robust Human Sensing
item.description:
Meeting room 5.1, Level 5. SMU SCIS 1, Singapore 178902 Tuesday, November 24, 2026, 5:45 - 6:45pm
Innovative Wearable Acoustic Sensing Mechanisms for Robust Human Sensing
Acoustic signals carry information about the human body through the sounds it generates and the changes it introduces to sound propagation. On wearable devices, these interactions provide opportunities to sense physiological activity and biometric characteristics during everyday use. Reliable sensing, however, requires addressing environmental interference, variations in available sound sources, and motion-related changes in sensing conditions. This dissertation investigates how complementary wearable acoustic sensing mechanisms can address these challenges for robust human sensing.
First, BreathPro captures body-generated breathing sounds using in-ear microphones to recognize fine-grained breathing modes during running. It combines in-ear and out-ear recordings to reduce environmental interference. Second, LR-Auth adopts opportunistic listening, exploiting the ear canal’s modulation of existing environmental sounds or music to enable lightweight, implicit user authentication. Finally, the proposed work explores active acoustic probing to support more reliable physiological monitoring during motion.
More info: computing.smu.edu.sg…: https://computing.smu.edu.sg/newsletter/phd-dissertation-proposal-hu-changshuo-innovative-wearable-acoustic-sensing-mechanisms?newsletter

item.title: Towards Operationalizing Technical AI Governance
item.description:
Meeting room 5.1, Level 5. SMU SCIS 1, Singapore 178902 Wednesday, November 25, 2026, 9 - 10am
Towards Operationalizing Technical AI Governance
Generative and agentic AI systems are being deployed faster than the rules meant to govern them. Regulations, standards and government frameworks increasingly say what these systems should achieve: robustness, fairness, security across the AI supply chain, and meaningful human oversight. They rarely say how to turn those expectations into technical requirements, controls and evidence that can be checked in practice. This dissertation proposal addresses that gap. It argues that governance expectations must be translated into technical properties that fit the deployment context and can be traced back to the requirements they come from. These properties should be grounded in where risks arise in real systems and in how organizations actually encounter and control them.
The proposal develops this argument in stages. It first establishes what governance instruments actually expect of generative AI, by comparing government frameworks across regions. It then traces where security and safety risks originate in real systems, mapping threats to specific components of the large language model supply chain. This work informed Singapore’s Technical Reference TR 147:2026. Next, it examines how enterprises deploying agentic AI encounter and control these risks in practice. It finds that current safeguards focus on constraining agents rather than on assuring, containing and recovering from their actions, and that existing guidance is too high-level to apply directly. It also shows that deployment context should shape how systems are assessed, so that the evidence required scales with the risk of the use case. The proposed final study brings these threads together. It turns guidance clauses into testable properties and executable test cases for agentic systems, starting with the insurance sector. Overall, the work moves technical AI governance from stating what is expected towards producing evidence of whether it is met.
More info: computing.smu.edu.sg…: https://computing.smu.edu.sg/newsletter/phd-dissertation-proposal-jose-luis-luna-campoverde-towards-operationalizing-technical?newsletter=

item.title: Reinforcement Learning Methods for Safety-Aware Decision-Making
item.description:
Meeting room 4.4, Level 4. SMU SCIS 1, Singapore 178902 Wednesday, November 25, 2026, 2 - 3pm
Reinforcement Learning Methods for Safety-Aware Decision-Making
Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved strong results across robotics, algorithm discovery, and classical games. However, deploying RL in safety-critical domains requires policies that satisfy safety constraints in addition to maximizing reward. This thesis addresses three settings for enforcing such requirements: action constraints, which restrict the set of admissible actions at every step; cumulative cost constraints, which bound the expected cost accumulated over a trajectory; and state-wise constraints, which require every state the agent visits to be safe. Projection-based approaches to action constraints can be computationally expensive and hinder policy learning when proposed actions fall far outside the feasible action space. To address action constraints, we present FlowPG, which learns a mapping to the feasible action space, reducing reliance on computationally expensive action corrections. However, a key challenge in FlowPG is the generation of feasible samples for complex constraints. We therefore present CV-Flow, which trains the flow model using a constraint violation signal. For cumulative cost constraints, we present Budget-Conditioned Reachability RL (BCRL), which defines a reachability set conditioned on the remaining safety budget. This formulation decouples reward maximization from the cumulative cost constraint, resulting in non-adversarial optimization. For state-wise constraints, we learn a safety value function from offline data to estimate the set of state-action pairs from which the agent can remain safe indefinitely. This accounts for actions that appear safe immediately but can lead to unavoidable future violations. We provide theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation on a diverse set of tasks, including continuous control, offline safe-RL, and maritime navigation.
More info: computing.smu.edu.sg…: https://computing.smu.edu.sg/newsletter/phd-dissertation-defense-brahmanage-janaka-chathuranga-thilakarathna-reinforcement?newsletter

item.title: Optimization under Choice and Behavioral Response Models: Algorithms and Performance Guarantees
item.description:
Meeting room 5.1, Level 5. SMU SCIS 1, Singapore 178902 Wednesday, November 25, 2026, 3:30 - 4:30pm
Optimization under Choice and Behavioral Response Models: Algorithms and Performance Guarantees
Retailers deciding which products to offer and at what prices, and defenders allocating limited protection against boundedly rational attackers, must anticipate how people respond to their decisions. Logit-family choice models describe these responses well, but building them into optimization produces nonconvex and often NP-hard problems, which practice usually tackles with heuristics or local search that give no measure of the remaining error. This dissertation proposal shows that the difficulty has an identifiable structure, and that exposing it yields algorithms with provable performance guarantees. It answers three research questions, one for each kind of decision. Discrete assortment decisions admit exact methods and approximation guarantees. For continuous decisions such as pricing and security allocation, and for estimating the choice models themselves, the hard part can be confined to a few customer segments, attacker types, nests, or model parameters, so solutions can be certified as globally optimal within a stated tolerance. Decisions that mix binary and continuous variables admit approximations with an explicit bound on the loss. Eight manuscripts support the proposal, and their experiments show that the methods certify instances that standard solvers leave open.
More info: computing.smu.edu.sg…: https://computing.smu.edu.sg/newsletter/phd-dissertation-proposal-pham-hoang-giang-optimization-under-choice-and-behavioral?newsletter

item.title: Diffusion-Enhanced GFlowNet for Solving Vehicle Routing Problems
item.description:
Meeting room 4.4, Level 4. SMU SCIS, Singapore 178902 Thursday, November 26, 2026, 4 - 4:15pm
Diffusion-Enhanced GFlowNet for Solving Vehicle Routing Problems
Traditional neural solvers for solving vehicle routing problems (VRPs) often suffer from limited solution diversity, motivating the development of Generative Flow Network (GFlowNet)-based models. However, the effectiveness of these models is frequently constrained by insufficient flow expansion in high-reward regions, limiting their ability to distribute probability across promising solution routes. The deeper exploration could yield superior results. Diffusion models, in contrast, provide stronger structural guidance for exploration. These two paradigms are naturally complementary: GFlowNet can supply edge-level signals for diffusion to embed, while diffusion can guide broader exploration. Leveraging this synergy, we propose Diffusion-Enhanced GFlowNet (DEG), a novel framework that integrates GFlowNet with a diffusion model to encourage richer flow expansion toward high-reward regions and derive higher-quality solutions. Specifically, DEG exploits GFlowNet’s inherent diversity to generate edge-specific backward signals, applies the stochastic noise schedule of diffusion to perturb these signals, and then denoises them within the GFlowNet paradigm. To further improve scalability, we introduce a specialized decoder capable of dynamically adapting to diverse problem scales. Extensive experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets, including instances with up to 10,000 nodes, demonstrate that DEG consistently achieves favorable performance compared to baseline methods. The code is available at https://github.com/ZHANG-NI/DEG.
This is a Pre-Conference talk for The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026): https://neurips.cc/.
More info: computing.smu.edu.sg…: https://computing.smu.edu.sg/newsletter/pre-conference-talk-zhang-ni-diffusion-enhanced-gflownet-solving-vehicle-routing?newsletter

item.title: Beyond Biosignals: Earables and the Future of Physiological Intelligence
item.description:
Meeting Room 4-4, Level 4. SMU SCIS 1, Singapore 178902 Friday, November 27, 2026, 10:30 - 11:30am
Beyond Biosignals: Earables and the Future of Physiological Intelligence
We can measure the human body continuously, but how much do we truly understand about its physiology? Wearables generate unprecedented volumes of biosignals, yet these remain incomplete observations of the biological processes governing human health. The challenge is no longer simply collecting data, but extracting meaningful physiological understanding.
In this talk, I will introduce Physiological Intelligence: a vision combining next-generation earable sensing with foundation models. Drawing on a decade of research from eSense to OmniBuds, I will present advances in multimodal cardiovascular and respiratory monitoring, including applications in hypertension and COPD.
My central thesis is that physiological AI is a representation problem, not merely a scaling problem. Predicting biomarkers accurately does not necessarily mean understanding the biology that generates them. Progress requires representations that capture physiological dynamics, preserve biological relationships and generalise across individuals and conditions. I will challenge us to rethink what physiological AI should learn, and explore what it will take to move from measuring the body to truly understanding it.
More info: computing.smu.edu.sg…: https://computing.smu.edu.sg/newsletter/research-seminar-fahim-kawsar-beyond-biosignals-earables-and-future-physiological?newsletter

Fahim KAWSAR Professor of Mobile Systems School of Computing Science University of Glasgow
Fahim KAWSAR is Professor of Mobile Systems at the University of Glasgow and Founder and Chief Technology Officer of OmniBuds, a medical technology company developing ear-worn sensing and AI systems for cardiovascular health. He is also Founder and Chief Advisor of IchiZero, a Finnish educational technology company developing Bella, a physical AI learning platform for children.  He spent 15 years at Nokia Bell Labs, where he was a Bell Labs Fellow and Director of Device Research. He founded and led the Cambridge Research Lab, advancing research in human-centred computing and intelligent systems. Over the past two decades, his work has contributed to advances in the Internet of Things, mobile sensing and on-device AI, particularly Earable Computing, a field he has helped shape. Fahim has co-authored over 200 peer-reviewed publications and holds more than 50 patents. His work spans fundamental research and its translation into technologies with real-world impact. As Editor-in-Chief of IEEE Pervasive Computing and an international keynote speaker, he continues to help shape research in embedded intelligence, pervasive AI and intelligent health technologies.

item.title: Towards Memory-Augmented and Value-Aligned Language Agents
item.description:
Meeting room 5.1, Level 5. SMU SCIS 1, Singapore 178902 Friday, November 27, 2026, 1 - 2pm
Towards Memory-Augmented and Value-Aligned Language Agents
Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the development of intelligent agents that interact with users over extended periods. However, such agents face persistent challenges in retaining past experiences, reasoning about temporal relationships, and ensuring that their behaviour remains aligned with human values. Existing approaches often rely on limited context windows, unstructured retrieval, or implicit alignment mechanisms, making it difficult to support reliable long-term interaction and accountable decision-making.
This dissertation investigates memory-augmented and value-aligned language agents through three complementary research directions. First, it develops ARTEM, a biologically inspired episodic memory framework that enables agents to encode and retrieve events using temporal, spatial, entity, and content information. Second, it introduces VALVE, a runtime governance framework that represents human values through an explicit hierarchy and enforces them over recalled memories and generated responses. Third, it proposes PBTG, a probabilistic temporal reasoning framework that integrates fragmented and uncertain temporal evidence into a coherent belief state.
The research evaluates these approaches on episodic memory, value alignment, and temporal reasoning benchmarks, examining their effectiveness and limitations. Ongoing work further investigates persistent temporal belief representations and adaptive value specifications through i-VALVE. Collectively, the dissertation aims to advance the development of language agents capable of remembering past experiences, reasoning about events over time, and acting in accordance with explicit and accountable human values.

item.xCal:summary: Towards Memory-Augmented and Value-Aligned Language Agents
item.xCal:location: Meeting room 5.1, Level 5. SMU SCIS 1, Singapore 178902
item.xCal:description:
Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the development of intelligent agents that interact with users over extended periods. However, such agents face persistent challenges in retaining past experiences, reasoning about temporal relationships, and ensuring that their behaviour remains aligned with human values. Existing approaches often rely on limited context windows, unstructured retrieval, or implicit alignment mechanisms, making it difficult to support reliable long-term interaction and accountable decision-making.
This dissertation investigates memory-augmented and value-aligned language agents through three complementary research directions. First, it develops ARTEM, a biologically inspired episodic memory framework that enables agents to encode and retrieve events using temporal, spatial, entity, and content information. Second, it introduces VALVE, a runtime governance framework that represents human values through an explicit hierarchy and enforces them over recalled memories and generated responses. Third, it proposes PBTG, a probabilistic temporal reasoning framework that integrates fragmented and uncertain temporal evidence into a coherent belief state.
The research evaluates these approaches on episodic memory, value alignment, and temporal reasoning benchmarks, examining their effectiveness and limitations. Ongoing work further investigates persistent temporal belief representations and adaptive value specifications through i-VALVE. Collectively, the dissertation aims to advance the development of language agents capable of remembering past experiences, reasoning about events over time, and acting in accordance with explicit and accountable human values.

item.title: Advancing Android Security through Arm Virtualization Extension
item.description:
Meeting room 5.1, Level 5. SMU SCIS 1, Singapore 178902 Monday, November 30, 2026, 2 - 3pm
Advancing Android Security through Arm Virtualization Extension
Android malware use UI manipulation, multi-stage payload delivery and malicious native libraries to avoid detection and trick users to perform unintended actions. To protect users, we leverage on hardware virtualization features, such as the protected kernel-based virtual machine (pKVM), to isolate sensitive UI components against a kernel adversary. Second, we use a live thread analysis approach at the binary level, combining symbolic execution with runtime introspection to uncover hidden behaviors during execution.

item.title: Formal models are magic
item.description:
Meeting Room 4-4 Level 4. SMU SCIS 1, Singapore 178902 Tuesday, December 1, 2026, 10 - 11am
Formal models are magic
In this work, we investigate a variant of the Four Glasses Puzzle (FGP) through the lens of formal verification. Although the puzzle appears to be unsolvable at first glance, formal verification enables the discovery of a correct solution. We demonstrate how the model can be constructed and reduced through progressive abstractions, ultimately yielding a concise and comprehensible model that captures all possible puzzle configurations. To ensure computational efficiency, we introduce the Escape Game - an algorithmic construction that eliminates redundant cycles and facilitates strategy synthesis under imperfect information. Finally, by analysing the strategic capabilities of the player, we present a solution to the puzzle. The approach is formally defined and proven correct.

Laure PETRUCCI Professor University Paris 13
Laure PETRUCCI obtained her PhD in Computer Science from University Paris 6 in 1991. She then became associate professor in Evry. In 2003, she obtained a Full Professor position at University Paris 13. Her research takes place in the SAFER team of the LIPN laboratory. Her area of expertise is formal specification and verification of concurrent systems so as to guarantee their appropriate behaviour, using automata or Petri nets models, as well as parametric models. In order to tackle the well-known state space explosion problem, the research she develops exploits modularity in the models, proposes distributed approaches, and algorithms for parameter synthesis. In recent works she has tackled strategy synthesis for multi-agent systems, according to different semantics, and proposed novel logics to express properties and model-checking approaches.

item.title: Process Discovery and Optimization from Relational Data
item.description:
Thursday, December 3, 2026, 10 - 11am
Process Discovery and Optimization from Relational Data
item.xCal:summary: Process Discovery and Optimization from Relational Data
item.x-trumba:customfield: SCIS EngD 2026 Dissertation Proposal by Joel Lim

Abstract Organizations generate large amounts of operational data across heterogeneous systems and relational databases. Although process mining provides established techniques for discovering and analyzing processes from event data, obtaining suitable process representations from relational databases remains challenging, particularly when process relationships, event sequences, and execution paths are not explicitly encoded in the underlying data. This dissertation investigates methods for deriving process knowledge directly from relational data with reduced reliance on manually defined process structures and data mappings. The first part focuses on identifying relationships across database tables and reconstructing process sequences from the resulting data dependencies and temporal information. The second extends this foundation through process routing discovery, examining how individual records traverse different process paths and identifying factors associated with particular routes or outcomes. The final part builds on the discovered process structures and routing information to investigate process optimization, with the aim of identifying inefficiencies, bottlenecks, and opportunities for improvement. Together, the research presents an end-to-end approach for transforming fragmented relational data into process representations and actionable process insights, supporting organizations in understanding how their operations are executed, how different process paths emerge, and where opportunities for improvement exist.
Speaker Biography Joel LIM is pursuing his engineering doctoral research at Singapore Management University in the area of process mining, discovery and optimization. His research focuses on enabling organizations to automatically uncover processes from relational data, understand how data and activities are connected, and ultimately identify opportunities for process optimization. His work bridges academic research with real-world business applications, particularly in complex financial and operational environments.

item.title: A Picture Is Worth a Thousand Tokens: Visual Communication for Human-AI Collaboration
item.description:
Meeting Room 4-4, Level 4. SMU SCIS 1, Singapore 178902 Tuesday, December 8, 2026, 11 - 11:30am
A Picture Is Worth a Thousand Tokens: Visual Communication for Human-AI Collaboration
Recent developments in generative AI have been changing how we live, work, and dream, revolutionizing many industries through their versatile capabilities. Humans bring goals, context, and judgement, while AI contributes speed, scale, and computational power. However, a major barrier to the fluency between humans and AI lies in communication, including expressing intent and understanding AI behavior. In this talk, I will share my perspective on the key considerations that shape effective human-AI communication via deliberately designed visualizations and interactions, through concrete examples spanning software development, graphic design, and beyond. These considerations offer a framework for thinking about how to design next-generation human-centered AI systems.

Jian ZHAO Associate Professor Cheriton School of Computer Science University of Waterloo
Dr. Jian Zhao is an Associate Professor in the Cheriton School of Computer Science, University of Waterloo, where he directs the WVisdom research lab. His research lies in the intersection of Information Visualization, Human-Computer Interaction, Data Science, and Human-Centered AI. He is dedicated to developing advanced interaction and visualization techniques that promote the interplay between humans, machines, and data. Dr. Zhao received his Ph.D. from the Department of Computer Science, University of Toronto, and joined the University of Waterloo in 2019 after working in the industry.   Dr. Jian Zhao has published over 100 peer-reviewed papers at prestigious venues in InfoVis, HCI, and other fields, winning numerous recognitions including five Best Paper, nine Best Paper Honorable Mention, three Best Poster/Demo (Honorable Mention) awards. He is also the recipient of multiple accolades such as the CS-Can|Info-Can Early Career Research Award (2025), Ontario Early Researcher Award (2025-2030), Outstanding Performance Award (2024), Cheriton Faculty Fellowship (2025-2028), and NSERC Discovery Accelerator Supplement (2020-2025). He is a Senior Member of ACM and IEEE. He has directly supervised five postdocs, 13 PhDs, 14 Master’s, and numerous undergrads, as well as mentored many PhDs during his tenure in industry and academia. He is an Associate Editor of IEEE TVCG. He has also served on the program committees of many world-class conferences such as IEEE VIS and ACM CHI, and has taken critical roles in the organizing committees of these venues such as ACM ISS’27 General Chair, IEEE PacificVis’26&27 TVCG Track Paper Chair, and ACM Alt.CHI’25 Paper Chair. Additionally, he has experiences at various industry research labs such as Microsoft, IBM, and Adobe, and holds over 20 granted patents. More information can be found on his website: www.jeffjianzhao.com.
